title: Pauri 16, meaning: the bull is dharma
hook: the earth is held not by a bull but by dharma, born of compassion; with one word the whole creation spread (Japji 16)

segments.voice: Yesterday, pardhaan, the foremost, and the sound of Pauri 16. Your line was panch parvaan: the chosen are accepted. Today, what the chosen understand.

Under the earth, a bull. That was one answer to an old question, what holds up the world, in the India Guru Nanak knew. The earth rests on the back of a great bull, the story went, and when it shifts its weight, the ground shakes. A picture of something strong underneath everything, carrying the load so nothing falls. Pauri 16 picks up that bull, turns it over in its hands, and gives it a new meaning.
screen: `A BULL UNDER THE EARTH.` → `WHAT HOLDS UP THE WORLD?` → `NANAK TURNS IT OVER.`

segments.voice: Yesterday we met the panch, the chosen ones, the people who have listened and trusted. Today the stanza tells us what they understand. Here's the line in the original: dhaul dharam daiaa kaa poot. Dhaul is the bull. Dharam is dharma, right living, the moral order. Daiaa is compassion, and poot is son. The bull is dharma, the son of compassion. The next line, in paraphrase: contentment, santokh, our word from Pauri 10, holds it patiently in place. So what holds up the world? Not an animal. Right living, born from compassion and steadied by contentment. Then the stanza asks the obvious question, almost with a smile. If a bull held up the earth, what would hold up the bull? Beyond this earth there are more earths, and more beyond those. What strength could carry all that weight? The bull can't be the answer; it just moves the question down one level. Then Pauri 16 widens out. All the beings, of every kind and color and name, were written by the ever-flowing pen. Who could ever write that account? With a single word, the whole creation spread out, and from it flowed countless rivers. It closes with a refrain we'll hear for four stanzas: what power do I have to describe it? Whatever pleases You is good. You are forever safe, Formless One. That's the understanding of the panch. The world stands on compassion, and it came from one word.
screen: `DHAUL DHARAM DAIAA KAA POOT.` · `WHAT HOLDS UP THE BULL?` · `ONE WORD, COUNTLESS RIVERS.` · `WHATEVER PLEASES YOU IS GOOD.` · then, large: `COMPASSION HOLDS THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Think of one act of compassion you could do, small and real, for someone who's tired, alone, or struggling with something you could lighten. Picture it: what you'd say, what your hands would do. Then breathe, feel the ground under you, and let it remind you what the stanza says holds it up.
Panch. The chosen ones of Pauri 16, who understand that the bull holding up the world is dharma, the son of compassion.
Your line: compassion holds the world. Not a bull: dharma, the son of compassion. Day one hundred eighty-eight, done.

howItsDone: Pauri 16 is recited each morning in Japji Sahib; its line dhaul dharam daiaa kaa poot is read in Sikh commentary as saying that the world is upheld by righteousness born of compassion.

beyond this earth are more earths; no bull could carry all that weight.

fork.setup: a friend asks you what holds up the world. you answer the way Pauri 16 does. what do you say?
options: dharma, born of compassion, steadied by contentment.
fork.reveal: dhaul dharam daiaa kaa poot: the bull is dharma, the son of compassion, and contentment holds it in place.

original.note: Gurmukhi, Japji Pauri 16: the bull is dharma, the son of compassion.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old myth about a bull under the earth.
what it means: what holds the world up is right living, born of compassion and steadied by contentment.
what a scholar hears: Guru Nanak takes a well-known cosmology and turns it into ethics; the refrain kudrat kavan kahaa veechaar begins here and closes pauris 16 to 19.
recall: fathomless, water too deep to wade across
the low, the bad, as in a bad mouth

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 3 (Japji, Pauri 16, the rest of the stanza and refrain)

notes: The earth-bearing bull is described as a belief people told in Guru Nanak's India (Puranic/folk cosmology), without a specific Puranic citation; confirm wording.
The mention of a turtle, giant or elephant in other cultures is a brief general note, not a comparison; confirm or remove.
Refrain paraphrased: what power do I have to describe it; whatever pleases You is good; You are forever safe, Formless One. Confirm.
The index word is panch while the teach is the bull; the script ties them by saying this is what the panch understand. Keeper may prefer a different word for this day.
